<!-- Generated from benchmark-strength.Rmd.orig by precompute/precompile.R. Edit the .orig file, not this one. -->



`bootmakr` reports the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable "as
strong as" an observed covariate been omitted. That phrase needs a
definition, and readers who are used to the impact threshold of a confounding
variable (ITCV) expect one in terms of correlations. The block that
`bootmakr` prints below its results gives it. This article explains what the
block contains, how to reproduce it, and what it should not be used for. (Why
the ITCV itself cannot serve as the definition when the regression uses
robust standard errors is explained in [Why bootstrap?](why-bootstrap.html).)

## Two relationships, two numbers

An omitted variable biases a regression coefficient only if it is related to
both the treatment and the outcome. `sensemakr` measures the two
relationships with partial R^2^ values (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020):

- the share of the variance of the **treatment** that the omitted variable
  explains, after the observed covariates have explained what they can;
- the share of the variance of the **outcome** that it explains, after the
  treatment and the observed covariates have explained what they can.

The square roots of these shares are the absolute values of partial
correlations. Nothing is known about an omitted variable, so the same two
numbers are computed for an observed covariate, the benchmark, and the
omitted variable is then assumed to be a multiple of it.

## The block

We use the data of the [worked example](ceo-pay.html): the effect of a
family CEO (`owner_ceo`) on the logarithm of CEO pay, with CEO tenure as the
benchmark and two multiples of it. The data come from the authors' OSF
repository.


``` r
library(bootmakr)
library(haven)

osf  <- "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
chen <- read_dta(osf)

ceo.model <- lg_ceopay ~ owner_ceo + ceo_tenure + PA_nic3_med + ceo_edu_dummy +
  lg_sales + firm_age + promoters_pct + institutions_pct +
  factor(year) + factor(nic_code_1digit)

out <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure", kd = c(0.5, 1),
                cluster = "co_code", reps = 100, seed = 123, progress = FALSE)

out$benchmark_strength
#> $type
#> [1] "single"
#> 
#> $observed
#>    benchmark   r2dxj.x    r2yxj.dx   r_dxj.x  r_yxj.dx
#> 1 ceo_tenure 0.1446519 0.003425632 0.3803313 0.0585289
#> 
#> $implied
#>    benchmark  kd  ky     r2dz.x     r2yz.dx    r_dz.x    r_yz.dx     r_yz.x
#> 1 ceo_tenure 0.5 0.5 0.08455735 0.002353248 0.2907875 0.04851029 0.08652389
#> 2 ceo_tenure 1.0 1.0 0.16911470 0.004836676 0.4112356 0.06954621 0.12013924
#>       impact
#> 1 0.02516006
#> 2 0.04940553
#> 
#> $r_yd.x
#> [1] 0.1394959
```



(The block does not depend on the bootstrap, so a small number of
replications is enough here.)

`$observed` describes the benchmark. CEO tenure explains
14.5 percent of the variance of family-CEO status
that the other covariates leave unexplained (`r2dxj.x`) and
0.3 percent of the variance of log CEO pay that the
treatment and the other covariates leave unexplained (`r2yxj.dx`). The
partial correlations are .38 and
.06: tenure is clearly related to who is a
family CEO and only weakly related to pay once family-CEO status and the
other controls are held fixed.

`$implied` describes the omitted variable that each row of the results table
assumes: its partial R^2^ with the treatment (`r2dz.x`) and with the outcome
(`r2yz.dx`), the corresponding partial correlations (`r_dz.x`, `r_yz.dx`),
its partial correlation with the outcome given the covariates *only*
(`r_yz.x`), and the product of that correlation with `r_dz.x`, the
`impact`. The printed block shows the two partial R^2^ values and the
impact. `$r_yd.x` is the partial correlation of the outcome with the
treatment given the covariates, which the impact calculation needs.

In Stata the same numbers are printed below the bootstrap table and returned
in `r(r2dxj_x)`, `r(r2yxj_dx)`, `r(impact)`, `r(r_yd_x)` and the matrix
`r(benchmark_strength)`.

## The impact of the omitted variable

The ITCV is stated as a product of two correlations of the omitted variable,
with the outcome and with the treatment, both taken given the observed
covariates (Frank, 2000). `sensemakr`'s two partial R^2^ values are almost,
but not quite, the squares of those correlations: the outcome relationship,
`r2yz.dx`, is measured given the treatment *as well as* the covariates. The
recursion formula for partial correlations removes the treatment from the
conditioning set,

*r*~yz·x~ = *r*~yz·dx~ √((1 − *r*~yd·x~²)(1 − *r*~dz·x~²)) + *r*~yd·x~ *r*~dz·x~,

where *r*~yd·x~ is the partial correlation of the outcome with the treatment
given the covariates, a quantity computed from the fitted model
(.14 here). The impact is then
*r*~yz·x~ × *r*~dz·x~.

One detail concerns signs. `sensemakr`'s bounds identify only the magnitudes
of the two correlations, and the sign of a hypothetical variable is
arbitrary. `bootmakr` takes *r*~dz·x~ as positive and gives *r*~yz·dx~ the sign
of *r*~yd·x~, which is the configuration in which the omitted variable biases
the estimate away from zero, the case that `sensemakr`'s adjustment removes
(with `reduce = FALSE` the sign is reversed). The impact therefore carries
the sign of the treatment effect, as the ITCV does.


``` r
r.yd <- out$benchmark_strength$r_yd.x
imp  <- out$benchmark_strength$implied
r.yz.x <- imp$r_yz.dx * sqrt((1 - r.yd^2) * (1 - imp$r_dz.x^2)) + r.yd * imp$r_dz.x
cbind(kd = imp$kd, impact = r.yz.x * imp$r_dz.x)
#>       kd     impact
#> [1,] 0.5 0.02516006
#> [2,] 1.0 0.04940553
```

The impact is on the same scale as a *conditional* ITCV, one stated in
partial correlations given the covariates. An ITCV in zero-order
correlations, the unconditional form that Lonati and Wulff (2026) use in
their simulations, would need the omitted variable's relationship with the
covariates as well; with a single control the assumption that the two are
unrelated suffices, with several controls it is a substantive assumption
that the sensitivity parameters do not identify. `bootmakr` therefore
reports the conditional impact only.

## Where the numbers come from

The observed strength can be reproduced from two regressions: the model
itself, and a regression of the treatment on the covariates.


``` r
fit   <- lm(ceo.model, data = chen)
fit.d <- lm(update(ceo.model, owner_ceo ~ . - owner_ceo), data = chen)

# benchmark with the outcome, given the treatment and the other covariates
sensemakr::partial_r2(fit, covariates = "ceo_tenure")
#>  ceo_tenure 
#> 0.003425632

# benchmark with the treatment, given the other covariates
sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.d, covariates = "ceo_tenure")
#> ceo_tenure 
#>  0.1446519

# outcome with the treatment, given the covariates (signed)
sign(coef(fit)[["owner_ceo"]]) * sqrt(sensemakr::partial_r2(fit, covariates = "owner_ceo"))
#> owner_ceo 
#> 0.1394959
```

A partial R^2^ of a single covariate is a function of its *t* statistic and
the residual degrees of freedom, *t*^2^ / (*t*^2^ + df), and the *t*
statistic used here is the conventional one. This does not make the block
depend on the choice of standard errors. The partial R^2^ is equally the
proportional reduction in the residual sum of squares when the covariate is
added to the model, a quantity that involves no standard error at all. The
*t* statistic is only a convenient way of computing it.


``` r
rss <- function(m) sum(residuals(m)^2)
1 - rss(fit) / rss(update(fit, . ~ . - ceo_tenure))
#> [1] 0.003425632
```

The implied strength of the omitted variable follows from the observed
strength of the benchmark. `kd` is defined as the variance of the treatment
explained by the omitted variable relative to the variance explained by the
benchmark, both measured after the *remaining* covariates have been taken
into account. Restating this as a partial R^2^ given *all* covariates,
benchmark included, gives


``` r
kd  <- c(0.5, 1)
r2d <- sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.d, covariates = "ceo_tenure")

kd * r2d / (1 - r2d)
#> [1] 0.08455735 0.16911470
```

which is the column `r2dz.x`. The corresponding value for the outcome,
`r2yz.dx`, is an upper bound that also depends on `ky` and on the benchmark's
relationship with the treatment. Cinelli and Hazlett (2020) derive both
expressions. This is why the omitted variable at `kd = 1` is somewhat
stronger than the benchmark itself in the block: the two are measured
against different sets of covariates.

`bootmakr` takes these values from `sensemakr`. You can obtain them directly:


``` r
bounds <- sensemakr::ovb_bounds(fit, treatment = "owner_ceo",
                                benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure",
                                kd = c(0.5, 1))
bounds[, c("bound_label", "r2dz.x", "r2yz.dx", "adjusted_estimate")]
#>       bound_label     r2dz.x     r2yz.dx adjusted_estimate
#> 1 0.5x ceo_tenure 0.08455735 0.002353248         0.2927133
#> 2   1x ceo_tenure 0.16911470 0.004836676         0.2541140
```

The last column is the adjusted estimate that `bootmakr` reports and
bootstraps.

## What the block is for

**It makes the assumption concrete.** "An omitted variable as strong as CEO
tenure" becomes "an omitted variable with an impact of
.05, a partial correlation of about
.41 with family-CEO status and
.12 with CEO pay". Readers can judge
whether that is a little or a lot in their field, and compare it with the
impact of observed variables.

**It describes the data, not the inference.** Every number in the block is a
function of the data alone. It is the same under conventional,
heteroskedasticity-robust and cluster-robust standard errors, and the same
in every bootstrap run. The problem that motivates `bootmakr`, that robust
standard errors change the *t* statistic on which the ITCV rests, does not
touch it.

**It is not a threshold.** The block does not say how strong an omitted
variable must be to overturn the result. That would require a critical value,
which brings the standard error back in. Whether a given strength overturns
the result is answered by the bootstrap confidence interval in the table
above the block, and the strength at which it first does so is the
[breakdown point](ceo-pay.html#the-breakdown-point). In particular, the
impact should never be compared with an ITCV computed from robust standard
errors, which is not a product of correlations at all.

## When the assumed strength is impossible

An omitted variable cannot explain more variance than there is left to
explain. If `kd` is so large that the implied partial R^2^ reaches 1,
`sensemakr` cannot compute the adjusted estimate. With CEO tenure as the
benchmark the limit is reached at `kd` = (1 − `r2dxj.x`) / `r2dxj.x`:


``` r
(1 - r2d) / r2d
#> ceo_tenure 
#>   5.913146
```



Well below that limit, the bootstrap runs into the same wall in some
replications and not in others, because the strength of the benchmark is
re-estimated in every bootstrap sample. `bootmakr` drops such replications
and reports how many failed. Here is a sweep that approaches the limit (200
replications keep it quick):


``` r
near <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                 benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure", kd = c(1, 3, 5, 5.5),
                 cluster = "co_code", reps = 200, seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
near
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo", 
#>     benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure", kd = c(1, 3, 5, 5.5), 
#>     reps = 200, seed = 123, cluster = "co_code", progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (200 reps, n = 2,011, 277 clusters)
#> Benchmark: ceo_tenure | kd = 1 3 5 5.5, ky = 1 3 5 5.5
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>                     Estimate  Std. Err       2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)  
#> owner_ceo (kd=1)    0.254114  0.117920   0.044595 0.474798   0.0517 .
#> owner_ceo (kd=3)    0.017287  0.206068  -0.364636 0.419972    0.793  
#> owner_ceo (kd=5)   -0.909475  0.738083  -2.105679 0.347583    0.569  
#> owner_ceo (kd=5.5) -2.353401 46.842693 -15.827437 0.309687    0.448  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Note: 84 of 200 replications failed and were dropped.
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                                Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> ceo_tenure with treatment | X      0.1447       0.380
#> ceo_tenure with outcome | D, X     0.0034       0.059
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>                    kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx Impact
#> 1.00x ceo_tenure 1.00 1.00 0.1691  0.0048  0.049
#> 3.00x ceo_tenure 3.00 3.00 0.5073  0.0173  0.136
#> 5.00x ceo_tenure 5.00 5.00 0.8456  0.0518  0.199
#> 5.50x ceo_tenure 5.50 5.50 0.9301  0.1002  0.210
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates. Impact: product of
#>  its partial correlations with the outcome and with the treatment, both given the
#>  covariates only, i.e. the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable
#>  biases the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the variance
#>  estimator, and not a threshold.)
```



The note below the table says that 84 of the 200 replications
failed. At `kd = 5.5` the omitted variable is assumed to explain
93 percent of the remaining
variance of family-CEO status; the adjusted estimate has become large and
negative, and its standard error is many times the estimate itself. Nothing
is wrong with the computation. The assumption is simply absurd for these
data, and the output says so in three ways: the failed replications, the
exploding standard error, and an impact (.21)
that no observed covariate comes close to.

Beyond the limit the full-sample estimate cannot be computed either, and the
call stops with `sensemakr`'s message:


``` r
beyond <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                   benchmark_covariates = "ceo_tenure", kd = 6,
                   cluster = "co_code", reps = 200, seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
#> Error in `ovb_partial_r2_bound.numeric()`:
#> ! Implied bound on r2dz.x >= 1. Impossible kd value. Try a lower kd.
```

The Stata command behaves the same way: failed replications are counted
below the table ("Warning: ... replications failed"; the number differs
because Stata draws different bootstrap samples), and a `kd()` beyond the
limit stops with error 3498, "Impossible value. Try a lower kd and/or ky". A few failures are of no concern. Many of them mean that the assumed
strength is near the limit of what the data allow, and that a smaller `kd`
or a weaker benchmark is the more informative question to ask.
